title: Chapter XXXIV
paragraphs: For several days after that evening, Mr. Heathcliff avoided joining us at meals, though he would not officially exclude Hareton and Cathy. He disliked giving in to his feelings so completely and preferred to stay away himself. Eating once in twenty-four hours seemed enough to sustain him.

One night, after everyone had gone to bed, I heard him go downstairs and out through the front door. I did not hear him return, and in the morning he was still absent. It was April then. The weather was gentle and warm, the grass as green as sun and showers could make it, and the two dwarf apple trees by the south wall were covered in blossom. After breakfast Catherine insisted that I bring a chair and sit with my work under the fir trees at the end of the house. She coaxed Hareton, now fully recovered from his accident, into digging and arranging her little garden, which Joseph's complaints had caused to be moved to that corner. I was comfortably enjoying the spring fragrance around me and the soft blue beauty overhead when my young mistress returned. She had run down towards the gate to gather primrose roots for a border, but came back with only half a load and told us Mr. Heathcliff was coming. “And he spoke to me,” she added, looking puzzled.
“What did he say?” Hareton asked.
“He told me to be off as quickly as I could,” she answered. “But he looked so unlike himself that I stopped for a moment to stare.”
“In what way?” he asked.
“Almost bright and cheerful. No, not _almost_ anything—_very_ excited, wild, and happy!” she replied.

“Then walking at night must amuse him,” I remarked, pretending indifference. In fact I was as surprised as she was and eager to see whether her report was true. A happy-looking master would be no everyday sight. I invented a reason to go inside. Heathcliff stood in the open doorway, pale and trembling. Yet there certainly was a strange, joyful glitter in his eyes that changed his whole face.
“Would you like some breakfast?” I asked. “You must be hungry after wandering about all night!” I wanted to find out where he had been, but did not like to ask directly.
“No, I'm not hungry,” he answered, turning his head away and speaking with some contempt, as though he guessed I was trying to discover the reason for his good mood.
I was puzzled and wondered whether this might be a suitable moment for a little advice.

“I don't think you should be roaming outdoors when you ought to be in bed,” I said. “At any rate, it's unwise in this damp season. You'll probably catch a bad cold or a fever. There's something wrong with you already!”
“Nothing I can't bear,” he answered, “and with the greatest pleasure, provided you leave me alone. Go inside and stop bothering me.”
I obeyed. As I passed, I noticed that he was breathing as rapidly as a cat.
“Yes,” I thought, “we're going to have an illness. I can't imagine what he's been doing.”
At noon he sat down to dinner with us and accepted a plate piled high with food, as though he meant to make up for his earlier fasting.
“I have neither a cold nor a fever, Nelly,” he said, referring to my morning's remark. “And I'm ready to do justice to the food you've given me.”

He picked up his knife and fork and was about to eat when his appetite seemed suddenly to vanish. He set them down, looked eagerly towards the window, then rose and went out. While we finished, we could see him pacing the garden. Earnshaw said he would go and ask why he would not eat. He thought we must somehow have upset him.
“Well, is he coming?” Catherine called when her cousin returned.

“Nay,” he answered, “but he's not angry. He seemed wonderfully pleased, in fact. I only made him impatient by speaking twice. Then he told me to go back to thee. He wondered how I could want anyone else's company.”

I put his plate on the fender to keep warm. An hour or two later, when the room was empty, he returned, no calmer than before. There was the same unnatural joy beneath his dark brows—and it _was_ unnatural—the same bloodless colour, with his teeth showing now and then in a kind of smile. His body shook, not with cold or weakness, but like a tightly stretched cord vibrating: a powerful quivering rather than a tremble.
I must ask what's wrong, I thought. Who else will? “Have you had some good news, Mr. Heathcliff?” I exclaimed. “You look unusually lively.”
“Where would good news come from for me?” he said. “It's hunger that makes me lively, and apparently I'm not to eat.”
“Your dinner is here,” I answered. “Why won't you have it?”

“I don't want it now,” he muttered quickly. “I'll wait until supper. And, Nelly, let me ask you once and for all to keep Hareton and the other one away from me. I want nobody troubling me. I want this place to myself.”
“Is there some new reason for banishing us?” I asked. “Tell me why you're behaving so strangely, Mr. Heathcliff. Where were you last night? I'm not asking out of idle curiosity, but—”

“You're asking out of very idle curiosity,” he interrupted with a laugh. “Still, I'll answer. Last night I stood at the threshold of hell. Today I can see my heaven. My eyes are fixed on it, scarcely three feet away! Now you'd better go. If you don't pry, you'll neither see nor hear anything to frighten you.”
I swept the hearth, wiped the table, and left, more bewildered than ever.

He stayed indoors for the rest of the afternoon, and no one disturbed him. At eight, though he had not called, I thought I should take in a candle and his supper. He was leaning against an open window ledge, but not looking outside: his face was turned towards the dark interior. The fire had dwindled to ashes. The damp, mild air of the cloudy evening filled the room. It was so quiet that I could hear not only the murmur of the stream down in Gimmerton, but its rippling and gurgling over pebbles and between the larger stones it could not cover. I exclaimed at the miserable state of the grate and began closing the windows one by one until I reached his.
“Shall I close this one?” I asked, trying to rouse him, for he had not moved.

As I spoke, the light flashed over his face. Oh, Mr. Lockwood, I cannot tell you what a fright that momentary glimpse gave me! Those deep, dark eyes, that smile, that deathly pallor! He looked to me like a goblin rather than Mr. Heathcliff. In my terror I tilted the candle towards the wall, and it went out, leaving me in darkness.
“Yes, close it,” he answered in his usual voice. “There, that's sheer clumsiness! Why were you holding the candle sideways? Hurry up and fetch another.”
I rushed out, foolishly terrified, and told Joseph, “The master wants you to take him a light and get the fire going.” Just then I dared not go back myself.

Joseph rattled some burning coals into a shovel and went in, but immediately returned, carrying the supper tray in his other hand. Mr. Heathcliff was going to bed, he explained, and wanted nothing to eat until morning. We heard him climb the stairs at once. He did not go to his usual room, but into the one with the enclosed bed. As I mentioned, its window is wide enough for anyone to climb through. I suspected he was planning another midnight outing and preferred us not to know.

“Is he a ghoul or a vampire?” I wondered. I had read of such hideous demons in bodily form. Then I reminded myself that I had cared for him as a child, watched him grow into youth, and followed almost his whole life. How absurd to give way to such horror! “But where did he come from, that little dark creature whom a good man sheltered to his own ruin?” superstition whispered as I drifted towards sleep. Half dreaming, I exhausted myself inventing a suitable parentage for him. Repeating my waking thoughts, I retraced his life with grim variations, finally imagining his death and funeral. All I remember of that is my great annoyance at being responsible for an inscription on his monument and consulting the sexton about it. Since he had no surname and we did not know his age, we had to content ourselves with the single word “Heathcliff.” That part came true. We did. If you go into the churchyard, you will find only that on his headstone, with the date of his death.

Daybreak brought back my common sense. As soon as there was enough light, I got up and went into the garden to look for footprints beneath his window. There were none. “He's stayed at home,” I thought, “and he'll be all right today.” I made breakfast as usual, but told Hareton and Catherine to eat before the master came down, since he was sleeping late. They preferred to take it outside beneath the trees, and I set out a little table for them.

When I came back, Mr. Heathcliff was downstairs. He and Joseph were discussing farm business. His instructions were clear and detailed, but he spoke rapidly and kept turning his head aside. His expression was as excited as before, even more so. Once Joseph left, he took his usual seat, and I put a bowl of coffee in front of him. He drew it closer, then rested his arms on the table and looked at what I thought was the opposite wall. His glittering, restless eyes travelled up and down one particular part of it with such intense interest that he stopped breathing for half a minute at a time.
“Come now,” I said, pushing some bread against his hand. “Eat and drink while it's hot. It's been waiting almost an hour.”
He took no notice, yet he smiled. I would rather have seen him grind his teeth than smile that way.
“Mr. Heathcliff! Master!” I cried. “For God's sake, don't stare as though you're seeing something from another world!”
“For God's sake, don't shout so loudly,” he replied. “Turn round and tell me: are we alone?”
“Of course,” I answered. “Of course we are.”
Even so, I found myself obeying, as though I were not quite certain. With a sweep of his hand he cleared a space among the breakfast things and leaned forward to look more freely.

Now I realised he was not looking at the wall. Watching only him, I could see he seemed to be gazing at something less than two yards away. Whatever it was apparently gave him pleasure and pain in their most intense extremes. At least, that was what his anguished yet ecstatic expression suggested. Nor did this imagined object stay still. His eyes followed it tirelessly and never left it, even when he spoke to me. I reminded him in vain how long he had gone without food. If my pleas moved him to reach for anything, if he stretched out a hand for bread, his fingers closed before reaching it and stayed on the table, their purpose forgotten.

I sat with exemplary patience, trying to draw his absorbed attention away from whatever held it. At last he became irritable and got up, asking why I would not let him take his meals in his own time. Next time, he said, I need not wait: I could set out the food and go. Then he left the house, wandered slowly down the garden path, and disappeared through the gate.

The hours dragged by in anxiety, and another evening came. I went to bed late, and even then could not sleep. He returned after midnight and, instead of going upstairs, shut himself in the room below. I listened and tossed about. At last I dressed and went down. Lying there, tormenting myself with a hundred groundless fears, was more than I could bear.

I could hear Mr. Heathcliff pacing restlessly, often breaking the silence with a deep breath that sounded like a groan. He muttered disconnected words too. The only one I could make out was Catherine's name, joined to some wild expression of love or suffering. He spoke as if to someone present, quietly and earnestly, with words wrung from the depths of his soul. I had not the courage to walk straight in, but wanted to draw him out of his trance, so I attacked the kitchen fire, stirring it and scraping the cinders. It brought him out sooner than I expected. He opened the door at once and said, “Nelly, come here. Is it morning? Bring your light in.”
“It's striking four,” I answered. “If you want a candle to take upstairs, you could have lit one at this fire.”
“No, I don't want to go upstairs,” he said. “Come in and make a fire for _me_. Do whatever needs doing in the room.”
“I must blow these coals red before I can carry any in,” I replied, fetching a chair and the bellows.
Meanwhile he wandered backwards and forwards, almost distracted, his heavy sighs coming so rapidly that there was hardly room for an ordinary breath between them.

“When it's light I'll send for Green,” he said. “I want to ask him some legal questions while I can still give those matters a thought and act calmly. I haven't made my will, and I can't decide how to leave my property. I wish I could wipe it from the face of the earth.”

“I wouldn't talk like that, Mr. Heathcliff,” I interrupted. “Let your will wait. You'll live to repent of your many injustices yet! I never thought your nerves would become unsettled, but they're terribly disturbed now, almost entirely through your own fault. The way you've lived these past three days could exhaust a Titan. Please eat something and get some rest. A look in the mirror would show you how much you need both. Your cheeks are hollow and your eyes bloodshot, like someone starving from hunger and going blind for lack of sleep.”

“It isn't my fault that I can't eat or rest,” he replied. “I assure you it's not deliberate. I'll do both as soon as I possibly can. But you might as well tell a man struggling in the water within arm's reach of the shore to rest! I must reach it first. Then I'll rest. Well, forget Mr. Green. As for repenting of my injustices, I've done no injustice, and I regret nothing. I'm too happy, and yet not happy enough. My soul's bliss is killing my body without satisfying itself.”
“Happy, master?” I cried. “A strange happiness! If you could listen without getting angry, I might offer some advice that would make you happier.”
“What advice?” he asked. “Tell me.”

“You know, Mr. Heathcliff,” I said, “that since you were thirteen you've lived selfishly, without Christian principles. You have probably hardly held a Bible in all that time. You must have forgotten what's in it, and perhaps you haven't time to examine it now. Could it hurt to send for someone—a minister of any denomination, it doesn't matter which—to explain it? He could show how far you've strayed from its teachings and how unfit you'll be for its heaven unless you change before you die.”

“I'm grateful rather than angry, Nelly,” he said, “because you've reminded me how I want to be buried. Have me carried to the churchyard in the evening. You and Hareton may come if you like. Above all, make sure the sexton follows my instructions about the two coffins! No minister need attend, and nothing need be said over me. I tell you, I've almost reached _my_ heaven. Other people's heaven has no value for me, and I have no desire for it.”
“And suppose you persist in this stubborn fast and die of it, and they refuse to bury you in the churchyard?” I asked, appalled by his godless indifference. “How would you like that?”
“They won't,” he replied. “If they do, you must have me moved secretly. Neglect it, and you'll have practical proof that the dead aren't annihilated!”

As soon as he heard the others stirring, he withdrew to his den, and I breathed more freely. But that afternoon, while Joseph and Hareton were at work, he came back into the kitchen. With a wild look, he told me to sit with him in the main room: he wanted company. I refused, telling him plainly that his strange words and behaviour frightened me, and I had neither the courage nor the wish to be alone with him.

“I believe you think I'm a fiend,” he said with his dismal laugh, “something too horrible to live under a respectable roof.” Then he turned to Catherine, who was there and had moved behind me when he approached. Half mockingly, he added, “Will _you_ come, pet? I won't hurt you. No! To you I've made myself worse than the devil. Well, there's _one_ who won't shrink from my company! By God, she's relentless. Oh, damn it! It's more than flesh and blood can possibly bear—even mine.”

He asked no one else for company. At dusk he went to his bedroom. All night and far into the morning we heard him groaning and murmuring to himself. Hareton wanted to go in, but I told him to fetch Mr. Kenneth, who should see him instead. When the doctor arrived, I asked to be admitted and tried the door, but it was locked. Heathcliff told us to go to hell. He was better and insisted on being left alone, so the doctor went away.

The next evening was very wet. Rain poured down until dawn. As I took my morning walk around the house, I saw the master's window swinging open and the rain driving straight inside. He can't be in bed, I thought: those showers would soak him through. He must be up or out. But I won't fuss any more. I'll go boldly in and look.

I got into the room with another key. Finding it empty, I hurried to open the panels of the bed. I pushed them aside and looked in. Mr. Heathcliff lay on his back. His eyes met mine so sharply and fiercely that I started, and then he seemed to smile. I could not believe him dead. But rain washed his face and throat, the bedclothes were dripping, and he was utterly still. The window, swinging backwards and forwards, had scraped one hand resting on the sill. No blood came from the broken skin. When I touched it, there could be no more doubt: he was dead and stiff!

I fastened the window, combed his long black hair back from his forehead, and tried to close his eyes. If possible, I wanted to extinguish that dreadful, lifelike stare of triumph before anyone else saw it. They would not close. They seemed to mock my efforts, and his parted lips and sharp white teeth mocked them too! Seized by another fit of cowardice, I called out for Joseph. He shuffled up and exclaimed, but absolutely refused to touch him.

“T' devil's carried off his soul,” he cried, “and he can have his carcass into t' bargain, for all I care! Ech! What a wicked one he looks, grinning at death!” The old sinner grinned back in mockery. I thought he meant to dance round the bed, but he suddenly composed himself, fell to his knees, raised his hands, and gave thanks that the rightful master and the old family had been restored to their rights.

The terrible event left me stunned, and my thoughts inevitably returned to earlier days with a heavy sadness. But poor Hareton, who had suffered the greatest wrong, was the only one who truly grieved deeply. He sat beside the body all night, crying bitterly. He held its hand and kissed the savage, mocking face everyone else shrank from looking at. His grief had the strength that comes naturally from a generous heart, even one as tough as tempered steel.

Mr. Kenneth could not determine what illness had killed the master. I concealed the fact that he had swallowed nothing for four days, afraid it might cause trouble. Besides, I am convinced he had not refused food deliberately. His fasting was the result of his strange illness, not its cause.

To the scandal of the whole neighbourhood, we buried him as he had asked. Earnshaw and I, the sexton, and six men to carry the coffin were the only people present. After lowering it into the grave, the six men left. We stayed to see it covered. With tears streaming down his face, Hareton dug squares of green turf and laid them himself over the brown earth. Now the grave is as smooth and green as the mounds beside it, and I hope its occupant sleeps as soundly. But ask the country people, and they would swear on the Bible that he _walks_. Some claim to have met him near the church, on the moor, even inside this house. Idle stories, you'll say, and I agree. Yet that old man by the kitchen fire insists he's seen two of them looking out of the master's bedroom window every rainy night since his death. And about a month ago something strange happened to me. I was going to the Grange one evening—a dark evening with thunder threatening—when, just at the turn by the Heights, I met a little boy driving a sheep and two lambs. He was crying terribly. I supposed the lambs were skittish and wouldn't go where he wanted.
“What's wrong, my little man?” I asked.
“Heathcliff and a woman are over there, under t' crag,” he sobbed. “I daren't go past them.”

I saw nothing. But neither he nor the sheep would go on, so I told him to take the lower road. He had probably imagined the phantoms while crossing the moors alone and thinking about the nonsense he had heard from his parents and companions. Still, I no longer like being out after dark, or being left alone in this grim house. I can't help it. I shall be glad when they leave and move to the Grange.
“So they're going to the Grange?” I asked.
“Yes,” Mrs. Dean answered, “as soon as they're married, which will be on New Year's Day.”
“Who will live here, then?”
“Joseph will look after the house, perhaps with a boy to keep him company. They'll live in the kitchen, and the rest will be closed up.”
“For whatever ghosts choose to occupy it?” I remarked.
“No, Mr. Lockwood,” Nelly said, shaking her head. “I believe the dead are at peace. But we shouldn't speak lightly of them.”
Just then the garden gate swung shut. The walkers were coming back.
“_They're_ afraid of nothing,” I grumbled, watching them approach through the window. “Together they'd face Satan and all his armies.”

As they reached the doorstep and paused for a last look at the moon—or, more accurately, at each other in its light—I felt an irresistible urge to escape them again. I pressed a small gift into Mrs. Dean's hand and ignored her protests at my rudeness. As they opened the front door, I disappeared through the kitchen. I would thus have confirmed Joseph's suspicions of his fellow servant's frivolous misconduct, had the pleasant ring of a sovereign at his feet not fortunately persuaded him that I was a respectable person.

I lengthened my walk home by turning towards the church. Beneath its walls I saw that decay had advanced even in seven months. Many windows had black gaps where the glass was gone, and here and there slates projected beyond the roofline, waiting to be loosened further by the coming autumn storms.

I looked for, and soon found, the three headstones on the slope beside the moor. The middle one was grey and half buried in heather. Turf and moss creeping around the foot of Edgar Linton's had only begun to blend it into the landscape. Heathcliff's was still bare.

I lingered beside them under that gentle sky, watching moths flutter among the heather and harebells, listening to the soft wind breathe through the grass, and wondering how anyone could imagine restless sleep for those lying in such quiet earth.
